doc.title: Billie Pierce and De De Pierce Interview, 1959-04-02

chapter: Florida bands and New Orleans comparison
title: Florida and Birmingham bands compared with New Orleans style; Lake Charles band
summary: Billie says Florida bands played jazz but with a different style from New Orleans, which Floridians loved, and recalls a trumpet-and-piano doubler from Lake Charles.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Mm-hmm. Well, can you tell us how did those bands compare with the, uh, well, when you came and played with Buddy Petit and heard some of the New Orleans bands, did they sound a good idea like the Florida bands or did they have a different swing to it? How did they sound?

Well, they all sounded all right to me. The same identical music because we saw swinging music, but the idea, just different faces. Yeah. It's different, you know, like a stranger come in. Well, she sure can play, he sure can play. That's it. Like it is right now. The music was the same, it's identical thing to me right then. You know, cause now, this Bebop stuff, I don't care, I don't use that, understand? But I'm just saying, well, that day, people was playing jazz. Yeah. Jazz, see, piano jazz, all that stuff.
But I wonder, did these Florida bands or the ones in Birmingham, did they sound about the same kind of, uh, Dixieland?

No, they sounded different. New Orleans style or different? No, different style all together. Different style, but they were playing jazz. But when the New Orleans, I don't know, New Orleans just had that regular swing. See, cause all them bands used to be in my hometown, and, uh, twice a week, different bands. They'd come over there. They would come with Buddy P.T. All Buddy P.T., did he come over there and play like this week, next week, because we had so many engaged, I mean places, but, um, we could put those bands. See? Yeah. Cause we had so many parks, see, and in the summertime, all our parks would be open up. See, we had parks on the water, bays, house, and everything like that, you see? Well, that's why he'll finish with music like that.
Did the people like those, uh, New Orleans bands better than the local?

They're still crazy about New Orleans bands. Uh-huh. They're still crazy about the music of New Orleans. And, uh, and then, uh, another fella, uh, this other fella was a great piano player I knew. That was, uh, uh, wait a minute, did he, what's Nelly Huston's name, Nelly Huston, I told you I knew him, you know? Charlie Seagher. Charlie Seagher, he was a great piano player. That was, uh, Nelly Lytton. Nelly Lytton, well I worked with us, you know, I worked with my band at one time.
Oh, I didn't know about him.

Yeah, well he got killed as a wreck. Yeah, yeah, yeah, you knew he was a trumpet band too. He was trumpet and piano, he was double trumpet and piano together. Oh, he was great. I never knew him. He came from Lake Charles, didn't he? That's right, that's where I formed a band in Lake Charles. Oh, Charlie Seagher, you know, Charlie Seagher, you know, he'd get, play trumpet with me and I'd play piano. Then he'd put the horn down, get on the piano, trumpet too and double ups. Double ups. Double ups, like that. That way he would work. Alternate, in other words. Alternate, just like that. Yeah.
